evidence.claim: From seaside cliffs to inland valleys, a coast road joined by bridges.

evidence.claim: Oregon’s Pacific Coast Scenic Byway follows US 101 between seaside cliffs, marshes, agricultural valleys and dunes, moving inland and back to the sea.
evidence.quote: The Pacific Coast Scenic Byway traces the entire Oregon coastline along Highway 101, bringing travelers to the sea and away again, winding past marshes, seaside cliffs, lush agricultural valleys, and wind-sculpted dunes.

evidence.claim: It is an All-American Road, whose coastal scenery, historic bridges and lighthouses feature in the Federal Highway Administration’s description.
evidence.quote: Pacific Coast Scenic Byway - Oregon All-American Road • Oregon

evidence.claim: whose coastal scenery, historic bridges and lighthouses feature in the Federal Highway Administration’s description.
evidence.quote: Charming small towns, museums, state parks, overlooks, historic bridges, and lighthouses ensure a delightful journey.

evidence.claim: Oregon’s transportation department recommends a minimum of ten to twelve hours of driving and several days for the trip.
evidence.quote: Minimum Drive Time: 10-12 hours; several days are recommended

evidence.claim: For most of its Oregon length, US 101 is an undivided two-lane highway, frequently mountainous between the ocean and Coast Range.
evidence.quote: Much of the highway runs between the Pacific Ocean and the Oregon Coast Range; thus, US 101 is frequently mountainous in character. For most of its length it is a two-lane undivided highway.

evidence.claim: Before the automobile highway, coastal travel depended on boats and beach routes.
evidence.quote: The Oregon Coast had historically been isolated and relied on boats and beach routes as their primary means of inter-city transportation.

evidence.claim: Approved in 1919 as the Roosevelt Coast Military Highway, the road entered construction in 1921 and became part of US 101 in 1926.
evidence.quote: formalized as the Roosevelt Coast Military Highway, which was approved for construction in 1919

evidence.claim: the road entered construction in 1921 and became part of US 101 in 1926.
evidence.quote: Construction of the highway began in 1921 and was later designated as part of US 101 in 1926

evidence.claim: Six ferry crossings interrupted the highway; even extended state-run schedules failed to keep up with motorists.
evidence.quote: The highway originally had six ferry crossings at major rivers and bays that were operated by private companies until their acquisition by the state government in 1927. The state ran these ferries on extended schedules to cope with demand, but they proved inadequate for the growing number of motorists on the coast.

evidence.claim: Five bridges designed by state engineer Conde B. McCullough replaced ferries between 1934 and 1936, and the highway was declared complete that October.
evidence.quote: A set of five bridges designed by state engineer Conde B. McCullough and funded by the federal government's New Deal programs were constructed between 1934 and 1936 to replace the ferries. The Oregon Coast Highway was declared complete on October 3, 1936

evidence.claim: Start in Astoria and travel south through Seaside to Cannon Beach and Haystack Rock.
evidence.quote: Down Highway 101 is Seaside, a popular beach resort known for its promenade. A few miles south of Seaside you'll reach Cannon Beach

evidence.claim: Start in Astoria
evidence.quote: Your Pacific Coast Scenic Byway adventure begins in Astoria

evidence.claim: Cannon Beach and Haystack Rock.
evidence.quote: Haystack Rock, a 235-foot monolith, towers over the beach

evidence.claim: The road turns inland toward Tillamook, then returns to the coast north of Lincoln City.
evidence.quote: After wending through deep forests, the Byway returns to the coast just north of Lincoln City.

evidence.claim: The road turns inland toward Tillamook
evidence.quote: The road then drifts slightly inland to Tillamook

evidence.claim: Continue through Newport and Yachats to Cape Perpetua, then Florence and the dunes.
evidence.quote: The Byway hugs the coast, passing through the small towns of Waldport, about halfway down the coast, and Yachats. Just below Yachats you'll come upon Cape Perpetua

evidence.claim: Continue through Newport and Yachats
evidence.quote: Next, you'll reach Newport

evidence.claim: then Florence and the dunes.
evidence.quote: South of Florence the rugged coastline gives way to 47 miles of gently rolling dunes that extend nearly to Coos Bay

evidence.claim: Farther south come Coos Bay, Bandon, Gold Beach at the Rogue River’s mouth, and Brookings.
evidence.quote: Down the coast at Gold Beach, the legendary Rogue River meets the Pacific.

evidence.quote: Returning to Highway 101, you'll soon reach the quaint coastal village of Bandon

evidence.quote: Finally, you'll reach Brookings.

evidence.claim: In Newport, Yaquina Bay Lighthouse combines its light and living quarters in one building.
evidence.quote: The Yaquina Bay structure is the only existing lighthouse in the state in which the living quarters are housed in the same building as the light.

evidence.claim: In Newport, Yaquina Bay Lighthouse combines its light and living quarters in one building.
evidence.quote: soon after the founding of the city of Newport, Oregon

evidence.claim: At Cannon Beach, a 235-foot basalt sea stack rises beside the beach.
evidence.quote: Haystack Rock is a 235 ft-tall (72 m) sea stack in Cannon Beach, Oregon.

evidence.claim: a 235-foot basalt sea stack
evidence.quote: Measuring 235 feet (72 m) tall, Haystack Rock is composed of basalt

evidence.claim: Haystack Rock was once connected to the coast; erosion separated it from the mainland.
evidence.quote: Haystack Rock was once joined to the coastline but years of erosion have since separated the monolith from the coast.

evidence.claim: At low tide, a strip of rock and sand connects the beach to the stack, with tide pools holding sea anemones, crabs, limpets and sea slugs.
evidence.quote: The Haystack Rock tide pools are home to many intertidal animals, including starfish, sea anemone, crabs, chitons, limpets, and sea slugs.

evidence.claim: At low tide, a strip of rock and sand connects the beach to the stack
evidence.quote: Visitors to Haystack Rock can view many species of marine wildlife in their natural habitat during low tide. The thin strip of rock and sand that connects it to the beach at these times features many tide pools.

evidence.claim: The rock also provides nesting sites for seabirds, including puffins.
evidence.quote: The rock is also a nesting site for many sea birds, including terns and puffins.

evidence.claim: Three smaller formations to the south are called the Needles.
evidence.quote: Three smaller, adjacent rock formations to the south of Haystack Rock are collectively called "The Needles".

evidence.claim: Oregon granted Haystack Rock Marine Garden status in 1990; the stack also lies within the Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge’s designated wilderness.
evidence.quote: In 1990, Haystack Rock was granted Marine Garden status by the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. The site is protected under the Oregon Islands National Wildlife Refuge as a designated wilderness area.

evidence.claim: The three smaller rock formations south of Haystack Rock are the Needles.
evidence.quote: Three smaller, adjacent rock formations to the south of Haystack Rock are collectively called "The Needles".

evidence.claim: A road cut into Cape Perpetua’s cliff opened travel between Yachats and Florence in 1914.
evidence.quote: In 1914, the United States Forest Service cut a narrow road into the cliff around Cape Perpetua and constructed a wooden bridge across the Yachats River, opening travel between the small community of Yachats and Florence to the south.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service paired that narrow road with a wooden bridge across the Yachats River; the bridge was replaced with steel in 1926.
evidence.quote: The wooden bridge was replaced in 1926 with a steel structure.

evidence.claim: The highway section followed in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: The Cape Perpetua section of the Roosevelt Memorial Highway (now Highway 101) was built in the 1930s.

evidence.claim: This forested headland rises above 800 feet.
evidence.quote: At its highest point, Cape Perpetua rises to over 800 feet (244 m) above sea level.

evidence.claim: On a clear day, the crest offers a view along 70 miles of Oregon coastline.
evidence.quote: From its crest, an observer can see 70 miles (113 km) of Oregon coastline and as far as 37 miles (60 km) out to sea on a clear day.

evidence.claim: The Civilian Conservation Corps built trails and the West Shelter observation point near the top; during World War II, that shelter served as a coastal watch station.
evidence.quote: The CCC constructed the Cape Perpetua campground, a network of trails, and the West Shelter observation point near the top of the cape. During World War II, the West Shelter observation point was used as a coastal watch station

evidence.claim: South of Florence, the coastal landscape opens into dunes, some reaching 500 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: with some dunes reaching 500 feet (150 m) above sea level.

evidence.claim: South of Florence, the coastal landscape opens into dunes
evidence.quote: South of Florence the rugged coastline gives way to 47 miles of gently rolling dunes

evidence.claim: The national recreation area stretches approximately 40 miles between Florence and North Bend.
evidence.quote: stretching approximately 40 miles (64 km) north of the Coos River in North Bend to the Siuslaw River in Florence

evidence.claim: Oregon’s transportation department describes sand derived from eroded mountain rock, carried to the ocean and washed inland by tides.
evidence.quote: The mounds of cream-colored, ever-shifting sand were created over millions of years as sedimentary rock from nearby mountains began to erode and particles were carried to the ocean. In time the particles became sand and were washed inland by the tides.

evidence.claim: The moving sand also entered literature: Frank Herbert’s research and fascination with this area helped inspire his science-fiction novel Dune.
evidence.quote: Frank Herbert's science-fiction novel Dune was partly inspired by the author's research on and fascination with the area.

evidence.claim: A national recreation area was established in 1972, protecting 32,186 acres under legislation sponsored by Congressman John R. Dellenback; it remains administered by the Forest Service.
evidence.quote: Pub. L. 92–260, sponsored by Congressman John R. Dellenback, was enacted in 1972, protecting 32,186 acres (13,025 ha) as the Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area.

evidence.claim: it remains administered by the Forest Service.
evidence.quote: It is part of Siuslaw National Forest and is administered by the United States Forest Service.
